cards.text: The prophet Ezekiel tells us that in the twenty-fifth year of exile, at the beginning of the year, on the tenth day of the month, fourteen years after Jerusalem was struck down, the hand of the LORD is upon him and He takes him somewhere. The twenty-fifth YEAR, friend. I spent years in a junk drawer, and by the end I was giving the dust names.

cards.question: In visions of God, where does the LORD take the exiled Ezekiel?

cards.text: He sets Ezekiel on a very high mountain, with something built on its southern slope. A VERY high mountain. Me, I have to hop, base and all, just to see over a mixing bowl.

cards.question: On the mountain's southern slope, Ezekiel sees a structure that resembles a ___.

cards.text: So He takes Ezekiel there, and a man is standing in the gateway. One look at this man and you know he is NOT your regular tour guide, and this tour is going to be ALL about the numbers.

cards.question: The man standing in the gateway has an appearance like ___.
The bronze-looking man in the gateway is holding something in his hand. What is it?

answers.text: A linen cord and a measuring rod
A scroll and a writing reed
A trumpet and a burning lamp

cards.text: Then the man tells Ezekiel, “look with your eyes, hear with your ears,” and pay attention to everything he's about to show him, because that's why Ezekiel has been brought here. I half-listened to an oven timer once, friend, and I'm STILL scraping that batch off the pan.

cards.question: The man tells Ezekiel to keep everything he sees to himself.
Instead, the man tells Ezekiel to report everything he sees to the house of ___.

cards.text: So Ezekiel starts looking. The first thing he sees is a wall running all the way around.

cards.question: What does the wall Ezekiel sees surround?

cards.text: The man's measuring rod is six long cubits, and the wall comes out one rod thick and one rod high. This man measures EVERYTHING. Me? My measuring is a scoop, a squint and a prayer.

Then he measures the gates, one by one: the gates facing east, north and south, and across the outer court with its thirty chambers, a gate into the inner court a hundred cubits from each one. They all have windows all around and palm trees on their side pillars, with seven steps up to the outer gates on the north and south and eight up to the inner gates. And every gate he measures comes out fifty cubits long and twenty-five wide. I've been trying to stamp two cookies the same since before the drawer, and this man gets SIX gates to match.

In each of the inner gateways, by the portico, there's a chamber with a doorway, and it's there for a job with the offerings. Every room in this place has a purpose. My old junk drawer had one purpose too: holding everything that didn't have one.

cards.question: In the chamber by each inner gateway's portico, the ___ offering was to be washed.
Inside the portico of the gateway are two tables on each side. What were those tables for?

cards.text: Count them up: four tables inside the gateway and four outside by the north gate, eight in all. There are also four tables of dressed stone holding the tools for the sacrifices, and in the inner court there are two chambers: one beside the north gate facing south, and one beside the south gate facing north.

cards.question: The man says the two chambers in the inner court are for priests. What do the priests in the south-facing chamber keep charge of?
The man says the north-facing chamber is for the priests who keep charge of the altar.
The priests in both chambers are the sons of ___, the only Levites who may approach the LORD to minister before Him.

cards.text: Zadok was a priest back in King David's day (2 Samuel 8:17), and here his family is still going by HIS name. I know the feeling, friend: the Millers carved “Dorin” on my handle, and I asked an ANGEL to let me keep it.
Next the man measures the inner court: square, a hundred cubits long and a hundred wide. SQUARE. My cookies are supposed to be round, friend, and some days they can't even pull THAT off.

cards.question: In that square inner court, the ___ was in front of the temple.

cards.text: Then the man brings Ezekiel to the portico of the temple itself. It's twenty cubits wide and twelve cubits deep, with steps leading up to it.

cards.question: How many steps lead up to the portico of the temple?

cards.text: There's a column by the side pillars, one on each side, and that's where we'll leave Ezekiel for now. Don't go anywhere, friend, because this tour is just getting started.

findings.problem: The line "this tour is going to be ALL about the numbers" points straight at the measuring rod, which is the answer to the choice card two cards later (card 7). It rules out the scroll and the trumpet before the baker picks.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later. Once a choice has been answered, the cards after it can build on that answer. A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The question opens with "Instead," which only makes sense next to card 9's true/false statement. Card 9 isn't on screen anymore, and on the correction round card 9 may come back after this card.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: No earlier card mentions a temple. Card 4 has just taught that the structure resembles a city, so a thoughtful baker would reason toward "The city of Jerusalem" over "The temple area." The right answer is luck.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: "The city of Jerusalem" is arguable as right. Card 4 established a city-like structure, and the wall surrounds that structure. The text never says the place is not Jerusalem.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The story card has four sentences: "The man's measuring rod...", "This man measures EVERYTHING.", "Me?" and "My measuring is..."

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The long-stretch summary goes nearly item by item: gate directions, thirty chambers, the hundred cubits between gates, windows, palm trees, seven versus eight steps, and fifty by twenty-five cubits. The first sentence is also hard to follow ("and across the outer court with its thirty chambers, a gate into the inner court a hundred cubits from each one"). It should say in a few words what the stretch covers, plus one standout detail.

rule.text: He says in a few words what it covers and doesn't go item by item. He can name a standout detail the text gives if it helps the stretch stick. The baker should know the stretch is there and what it's about, not memorize it.

findings.problem: The story card has three sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: "Every room in this place has a purpose" is presented as something the text shows. The passage gives no purpose for most rooms, such as the thirty chambers of the outer court (Ezekiel 40:17).

rule.text: Noticing. What he points out must be true.

findings.problem: One story card carries three beats: the count of the eight slaughtering tables, the four dressed-stone tables, and the two chambers in the inner court.

rule.text: Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.

findings.problem: The question says "The priests in both chambers are the sons of ___." In Ezekiel 40:46, "These are the sons of Zadok" comes right after the altar priests, and the text doesn't say it covers the priests of the temple chamber too. The card settles what the text leaves open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The joke compares Zadok's descendants being called by their ancestor's name with Papa Dorin keeping his own name. These are not the same action, so "I know the feeling" doesn't click. The card also doesn't move the passage forward; it only adds to verse 46, which card 7 already covered.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The story card has three sentences, counting "SQUARE."

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The number of steps up to the portico (ten) is a building measurement. Nothing on earlier cards lets the baker reason to it, so it's pure luck. It also isn't a detail the baker needs to understand the passage.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.
